claims.text: Adding a moderate amount of Zr to a metallic-glass precursor alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Zr addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Increased atomic-size mismatch disrupts crystalline nucleation.
A conventional binary or ternary Cu-based alloy can serve as a metallic-glass precursor with moderate glass-forming ability.
Zr addition increases atomic-scale disorder and packing frustration because of atomic-size differences.
Zr atoms are larger than the other constituent atoms in the proposed alloy.
Zr addition deepens the alloy's eutectic response.
Disruption of local atomic ordering reduces the likelihood of crystal nucleation during cooling.
Reduced crystal nucleation promotes glass formation.
A Zr-doped alloy will have a higher critical cooling rate than the undoped alloy.
The proposed higher critical cooling rate means that a slower cooling rate is sufficient to obtain a fully amorphous structure.
The effectiveness of Zr addition varies with alloy composition and cooling-rate thresholds.
Failure of Zr doping to lower the required critical cooling rate, increase amorphous fraction, or delay crystallization would falsify the enhancement hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction equates a higher critical cooling rate with the ability to form glass at a slower cooling rate. These directions are inconsistent: requiring slower cooling corresponds to a lower required critical cooling rate.
The predicted outcome specifies a higher critical cooling rate as improvement, whereas the falsification rule correctly treats a lower required critical cooling rate as improvement.
